newsitem.title: FRANCE: Anti-personnel mine makers seen evading planned ban.
newsitem.headline: Anti-personnel mine makers seen evading planned ban.

text.p: French pressure groups said on Thursday that producers and users of anti-personnel mines were finding legal ways of flouting a proposed ban on the weapons that maim civilians long after wars have ended.

The groups Handicap International and Observatory of Arms Transfers said new kinds of landmines presented as "intelligent systems" or "counter-demining devices" were effectively anti-personnel mines in disguise.
"Only the name has changed, this is hypocrisy," said Philippe Chabasse, head of Handicap International, which campaigns for a total ban on anti-personnel mines and helps civilians maimed by them.

More than 100 million landmines lie buried or hidden in 64 countries around the world. They are said to kill or injure one person in the world every 20 minutes, or 25,000 people a year, many of them children at play and farmers ploughing the fields.
Countries like Angola, Cambodia, Bosnia and Mozambique which suffered long and bitter civil wars are among the worst affected.
World powers are seeking a ban on anti-personnel mines, which explode underfoot, unlike anti-armour mines designed to go off under the weight of heavy vehicles.
Chabasse said modern anti-armour mines included sensitive triggers that could be set off by passers-by.
Counter-demining devices intended to hamper the removal of anti-armour mines were de facto anti-personnel weapons under another name, Chabasse said.
He said manufacturers sought to prevent long-life minefields through so-called "smart landmines" which self-destruct or are automatically defused after a certain time.
But they were not totally reliable and at least 10 percent of them failed to neutralise themselves, he said.

Chabasse voiced concern that a loophole had been opened in the proposed ban on anti-personnel mines by adding the word "essentially" to the definition of them, as "mines essentially designed to explode because of the presence, proximity of or contact with a person".
This could exclude from the ban certain types of mines, including booby-trapped ones, he added.
Major countries including the United States are seeking a global ban on anti-personnel landmines at the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva.
Canada is also trying to negotiate a ban through its "Ottawa process" of talks, in the face of opposition from Russia and China, the main global suppliers of landmines.

The two French groups accused France of dragging its feet in implementing pledges made since 1993 to outlaw anti-personnel mines, saying Paris had failed to enshrine into law its decision to ban production and export of the weapons.
The Foreign Ministry said a bill was being drafted, but gave no date for its presentation to parliament.
"Anti-personnel mines are a scourge. They must be outlawed, this is France's objective...Our country is spearheading the fight against anti-personnel mines," it said in a statement.
